newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli Arabs move to address parliament in Arabic.
newsitem.headline: Israeli Arabs move to address parliament in Arabic.

text.p: Arab members of Israel's parliament have decided to use the Arabic language to address the Jewish state's legislative assembly, an Arab lawmaker said on Tuesday.

"Arabic, Hebrew and English are the official languages in Israel, but for the past 30 years, Arabic has not been used in the Knesset (parliament) because Arabs themselves have neglected their rights," Abdel-Wahab al-Darawsheh of Israel's Arab Democratic Party told Reuters.
Darawsheh said Knesset Speaker Dan Tichon had agreed to fund translation of Arabic speeches into Hebrew for Jewish lawmakers.

"We have to inform him a few days in advance so that translation into Hebrew can be provided," Darawsheh said. "He has also approved buying Arabic newspapers for the library and to allow Arab journalists to attend Knesset sessions."
Darawsheh said the move "consolidates that Arabic is an official language and it also consolidates the Arab presence in the Knesset and in Israel".

Israeli Arabs, who have long complained of discrimination, have been more assertive in pressing for equality for Israel's 800,000 Arab citizens since winning an unprecedented 11 seats in the 120-member Knesset in elections last May.
Earlier in the year, Arab lawmakers demanded they be allowed to set up a mosque in the Knesset building for Moslem prayers.
"This was our first achievement and a room was set up as a mosque where we pray in the Knesset, just as the Jews have their own prayer places," Darawsheh said.
Darawsheh said some right-wing Jewish lawmakers strongly objected to the mosque opening and had heckled Arab parliamentarians who addressed the Knesset in Arabic.
"Some Jewish extremist Knesset members opposed both decisions, and one member submitted a stupid proposal asking the Knesset to cancel its recognition of Arabic as an official language," he said.
Israel granted citizenship to those Arabs who did not flee their towns and villages during the 1948 Arab-Israeli war after the founding of the Jewish state.
